Position: Address (setup).

What you’re doing well
- Balanced, athletic base with knees bent and feet shoulder-width — a good platform for rotation.
- Eyes down on the ball and chin up enough to allow shoulder turn.
- Club sits behind the ball in a controlled, neutral position (ready to swing).

What looks off
- Upper body appears a touch upright/hunched instead of a clear spine tilt from the hips, which can limit a full shoulder turn.
- Weight looks slightly back toward the heels rather than centered on the mid/balls of the feet — can cause early sway or inconsistent low-point.
- Hands/shaft could use a touch more forward lean for sharper iron contact (depending on club).

2–3 things to work on
1) Posture reset drill: Stand facing a mirror, tip from the hips until you feel weight on the balls of your feet, keep a slight knee flex and chest up. Hold 5–10 seconds and repeat until the hip hinge feels automatic.
2) Alignment/weight check: Place an alignment stick along your insteps and another under your toes to ensure weight is forward of heels. Make 10 slow setup reps without swinging, feeling the balance on the balls of your feet.
3) Forward shaft-lead: At setup, push your lead hip slightly toward the target and let your hands move a few inches ahead of the ball for a small forward shaft lean (iron-friendly). Practice with half swings to groove low-point control.

Repeat these setup reps before every range session to build a more stable, consistent address position.

Position: Top of the backswing.

What you’re doing well
- Good width to the swing — arms extended away from the body give a long arc and potential for power.
- Strong shoulder turn — upper body has rotated well away from the ball while keeping the head reasonably still.
- Balanced base — feet are planted and you look stable, which is a good foundation for the downswing.

What looks off
- Hands appear a little high and slightly behind the head, which can steepen the shaft and promote an "over‑the‑top" move or an open clubface at transition.
- Lower body looks a touch inactive/swayed to the trail side rather than coiling; that can delay the downswing sequence and reduce consistency.

2–3 specific things to work on
1. Pause-at-top drill: Make 3–5 half swings, pause and hold the top for one count. Check that your lead wrist is firm (not cupped) and the club shaft sits on a shallower plane. Hold the position until it feels connected to your torso.
2. Toe‑touch/step drill for sequence: From the top, step your trail foot slightly toward the target as you start down to feel the correct weight shift and hip lead — this promotes inside-to-out path and earlier lower‑body initiation.
3. Swing‑plane rod or alignment pole: Place a pole along your target line and swing so the shaft tracks slightly inside the pole on the downswing. Work slower repetitions to groove a shallower, more connected transition.

Do these drills for short practice sessions (10–15 minutes) and prioritize feeling the lower body lead and a connected top position.

Position: Top of the backswing.

What you’re doing well
- Good shoulder turn — torso has rotated well away from the target which stores power.
- Stable head/upper body — eyes appear steady over the ball, helping consistency.
- Strong wrist hinge — the club is up, showing good wrist set.

What’s off
- Lower body looks a bit soft/unstable: right knee and hip seem to slide laterally rather than coil, which can leak power and cause an inconsistent transition.
- Possible loss of connection between left arm and torso (left elbow appears bent/inward), which can lead to an open clubface or a steep downswing.

2–3 things to work on
1) Brace and coil the lower body: practice swings with feet shoulder-width and a slight knee flex; feel the trail-side load (right hip back) without sliding. Small-step drill: make a backswing and take a tiny step with the lead foot toward target on the start of the downswing to train weight shift.
2) Maintain connection of left arm to chest: do slow-motion half-swings keeping the left arm straight-ish and feeling it stay connected to the left pec — this promotes a wider arc and square face at impact.
3) Pause-and-check at the top: make practice swings where you hold the top for a second to self-check wrist angle and clubface position; then initiate a smooth rotation from the ground up.

Repeat drills slowly, then build speed while keeping the same positions.

Position: Address (setup) — the golfer is in the pre-shot setup with the club behind the ball.

What’s working
- Athletic posture: good spine tilt and a nice knee flex — looks ready to move.
- Balanced stance: feet around shoulder width which gives a stable base.
- Eyes down on the ball and a relaxed head position.

What’s off
- Hands look a little behind the ball (tendency to come under the ball at impact).
- Weight appears slightly on the back foot rather than slightly favoring the front foot for a solid iron strike.
- Shoulder/feet alignment looks a touch closed to the target — can encourage an inside-out path.

2–3 things to work on
1) Hands slightly forward at setup: shift your grip/handle 1–2 cm closer to the lead thigh so there’s a small shaft lean. This promotes crisp ball-first contact on irons.
2) Weight distribution check: set up with about 55% on the front foot (feel pressure on the inside ball of the lead foot). Practice rocking onto the front foot in a slow half-swing to ingrain the move.
3) Alignment drill: place an alignment stick along your toe line and another pointing at the target; square your shoulders and feet to the stick to avoid a closed stance. Repeat 10 times before hitting balls.

Optional drill: hit 50% swings while pausing at waist height to confirm hands stay ahead of the ball and weight is moving forward.
